desc:
For every node of a binary tree compute the sum of the distances (number of edges on the connecting path) from that node to every other node of the tree.

Return an array with one entry per real node, in the order in which the nodes appear in the level-order input (skip the -1 markers): ans[k] belongs to the k-th real node. Node values play no role and may repeat. The empty tree gives [].

How trees are given. There is no tree type here. A binary tree is passed as an integer array in level-order (top to bottom, left to right). A missing child is written as -1, and every real node value is non-negative. The children of a missing node are not listed, and trailing -1 entries are dropped, so a non-empty array never ends with -1. The empty tree is [].

For example, [1, 2, 3, -1, 4] describes the tree on the left: the root is 1 with children 2 and 3, node 2 has no left child and has 4 as its right child, and node 3 is a leaf.

    1
   / \
  2   3
   \
    4

For tree = [1, 2, 3] the answer is [2, 3, 3]: from the root both nodes are at distance 1; from node 2 the root is at distance 1 and node 3 at distance 2. For tree = [5, 5, -1, 5] (a chain of three nodes) the answer is [3, 2, 3].
constraints: The array follows the encoding above exactly (valid level-order, no trailing -1)
hints: Running a search from every node costs O(n) each, which is O(n<sup>2</sup>) overall. With n = 1,500 that is borderline, and the idea matters more: reuse work between neighbouring nodes.
Compute the answer for the root with one traversal, and compute subtree sizes at the same time. Then think about how the answer changes when you move from a node to one of its children.

Moving from a parent p to its child c brings the size[c] nodes of c's subtree one step closer and pushes the other n - size[c] nodes one step farther: ans[c] = ans[p] - size[c] + (n - size[c]). The root's answer is the sum of all depths.
editorial: This is the classic re-rooting technique. First compute size[k], the number of nodes in the subtree of k, bottom-up, and the answer of the root, which is simply the sum of all depths.

Now go top-down. Take a node p with known answer and its child c. Compared with standing at p, standing at c shortens the distance by 1 to each of the size[c] nodes inside c's subtree and lengthens it by 1 to each of the other n - size[c] nodes. Hence ans[c] = ans[p] - size[c] + (n - size[c]). Because the level-order array lists parents before children, both passes are plain loops over the nodes: O(n) time and space.
The largest possible value is about n<sup>2</sup>/2 ≈ 1.1 million for a chain of 1,500 nodes, comfortably inside 32 bits.
